ELECTIVE AREA 2 · JUNE

Mathematical games

Seven pieces, one square. Seven pieces, one cube. A tower that has to move house, and a little pile of sticks where you can work out the win in advance. In this chapter you lay, slide, move and roll – and find out what mathematics is hidden in the games. At the end you invent a game of your own.

  • make shapes from tangram pieces and the Soma cube and compare areas
  • solve sliding puzzles and the Tower of Hanoi and predict the number of moves
  • find a winning strategy for the Nim game
  • count chances in dice games and design a game of your own

UNIT 13 LESSONS

1Tangram and Soma cube

The tangram is an old Chinese shape puzzle: a square is split into seven pieces – five triangles, one square, one parallelogram. You make shapes out of them. The rule: all seven pieces are used, and none lies on top of another.

Because all the pieces are always used, every tangram shape has the same area as the square – whether cat or boat. Only the perimeter changes.

The Soma cube is the three-dimensional counterpart: seven pieces made of 27 small cubes form a 3 × 3 × 3 cube. One piece has 3 cubes, the other six have 4 each.

KEY POINT · SHAPE PUZZLES

Tangram: 2 large, 1 medium, 2 small triangles, 1 square, 1 parallelogram. Shares: $\tfrac{1}{4}$, $\tfrac{1}{8}$, $\tfrac{1}{16}$

Equal by dissection: shapes made of the same pieces have the same area.

Soma cube: 7 pieces, $3 + 6 \cdot 4 = 27$ small cubes

Comparing: the square, the parallelogram and the medium triangle are the same size – two small triangles fit exactly into each.

Invented in a lecture hall: Piet Hein thought up the Soma cube in 1933 during a lecture by Werner Heisenberg.

INTERACTIVE · THE SEVEN PIECES

Tap a piece: you see its name, its share of the square and which pieces are the same size.

EXAMPLE 1 · SHARES

The tangram square has a side length of 16 cm. How big is a large triangle, and how big is a small one?

Square: $16 \cdot 16 = 256$ cm². Large triangle: $\tfrac{1}{4}$ of it, small triangle: $\tfrac{1}{16}$.

64 cm² and 16 cm²

EXAMPLE 2 · THE SAME AREA

A cat is made from all seven pieces of an 8 cm tangram. What area does the cat have?

All the pieces, nothing on top of each other: the same area as the square.

64 cm²

EXERCISES

Count the pieces of the tangram: how many triangles, how many quadrilaterals? Which quadrilaterals are they?

5 triangles, 2 quadrilaterals: a square and a parallelogram.

Use the two small triangles to make a) a square   b) a parallelogram   c) a triangle. What do the three shapes have in common?

All three have the same area: $\tfrac{1}{8}$ of the tangram square. The triangle is exactly as big as the medium triangle.

The tangram square has a side length of 12 cm. Calculate the area of each piece. Check whether they add up to 144 cm² altogether.

large triangles 36 cm² each, medium triangle, square and parallelogram 18 cm² each, small triangles 9 cm² each. $2 \cdot 36 + 3 \cdot 18 + 2 \cdot 9 = 144$ ✓

The Soma cube has 7 pieces. How many small cubes does the smallest piece have if all the others have 4? Why can there not be a piece of only 2 cubes if all the others have 4?

$27 - 6 \cdot 4 = 3$. With a piece of two and six pieces of four there would only be $2 + 24 = 26$ cubes – one would be missing.

TEST YOURSELF!

What fraction of the tangram square is the parallelogram?

as big as two small triangles: $\tfrac{1}{8}$

A square with a 16 cm side: area of a large triangle in cm²?

$256 : 4 = 64$

How many pieces does the Soma cube consist of?

7

UNIT 22 LESSONS

2Sliding puzzle and Tower of Hanoi

In a sliding puzzle, numbered tiles lie in a frame, and one space is empty. You slide tiles into the gap until the numbers are in order. In the Tower of Hanoi, a tower of discs has to move to another peg – disc by disc, never a larger one on a smaller one.

For the tower, reducing it to something familiar helps: to move 4 discs, you first put the top 3 to one side, then the largest disc on the target, then the 3 on top of it. So if you can do 3 discs, you can also do 4.

This creates a pattern: 1 disc needs 1 move, 2 discs need 3, 3 discs 7, 4 discs 15. Each time double and add 1.

KEY POINT · TOWER OF HANOI

Strategy: top tower out of the way, largest disc on the target, top tower on top

Least number of moves: 1, 3, 7, 15, 31, … · next number = $2 \cdot \text{previous} + 1$

With $n$ discs: $2^n - 1$ moves

The legend of 64 golden discs was invented by Édouard Lucas in 1883 along with the puzzle. At one move per second, moving them would take more than 500 billion years.

Sliding puzzle: if you swap two tiles, it cannot be solved. W. W. Johnson and W. E. Story proved this in 1879.

INTERACTIVE · THE TOWER OF HANOI

Move the tower from A to C. Can you do it with the least number of moves? “Show solution” demonstrates the strategy.

INTERACTIVE · THE SLIDING PUZZLE

Put the tiles in order. Hint: sort out the top row first and then do not touch it any more.

EXAMPLE 3 · PREDICTING MOVES

What is the least number of moves needed for 5 discs?

4 discs: 15 moves. Then $2 \cdot 15 + 1 = 31$. Check: $2^5 - 1 = 32 - 1 = 31$.

31 moves

EXAMPLE 4 · THE LARGEST DISC

With 4 discs, how often does the largest disc move, and how often the smallest?

The largest only once. The smallest on every second move: moves 1, 3, 5, …, 15.

largest once, smallest 8 times

EXERCISES

Solve the tower with 3 discs in the interactive element in 7 moves. Write down the moves (for example A → C).

A → C, A → B, C → B, A → C, B → A, B → C, A → C

Continue the sequence: 1, 3, 7, 15, … What is the rule?

31, 63, 127. Rule: double and add 1.

One move takes 2 seconds. How long does moving 6 discs take? And 10 discs?

6 discs: 63 moves, 126 s = 2 min 6 s. 10 discs: 1023 moves, 2046 s ≈ 34 min.

In the 8-tile sliding puzzle everything is in place, only 7 and 8 are swapped. Solve it with the interactive element – or explain why it does not work.

It does not work. With legal moves you never get to a position where only two tiles are swapped (Johnson and Story, 1879). That is why the interactive element only shuffles with legal moves.

TEST YOURSELF!

Least number of moves with 5 discs?

$2 \cdot 15 + 1 = 31$

Least number of moves with 6 discs?

$2 \cdot 31 + 1 = 63$

4 discs: how often does the smallest disc move?

on every second of the 15 moves: 8 times

UNIT 32 LESSONS

3Nim games: working out the win in advance

21 sticks lie on the table. Two people take turns, and each takes 1, 2 or 3 sticks. Whoever takes the last one wins. Sounds like luck – but it is not. If you think backwards, you can predict the outcome.

Thinking backwards: if there are still 1, 2 or 3 sticks, you take them all and win. If there are 4, you have lost: whatever you take, the other person takes the rest. So you want to leave your opponent 4. The same goes for 8, 12, 16, 20 – all multiples of 4.

With 21 sticks you therefore take 1 first (20 are left). After that you always make your opponent’s move up to 4: if they take 3, you take 1; if they take 2, you take 2.

KEY POINT · WINNING STRATEGY

Rule: take 1 to 3 sticks, whoever takes the last one wins

Winning positions: leave your opponent a multiple of 4 · after that always make it up to 4

If there is already a multiple of 4 at the start, the second player wins with the best play.

Divide with remainder: you find the first move with the remainder when dividing by 4: 21 : 4 = 5 remainder 1 → take 1.

A different rule? If you may take 1 to 5, you make it up to 6.

INTERACTIVE · NIM AGAINST THE COMPUTER

You start. Can you beat the computer? With “show the fours” you see the groups counted from the end.

EXAMPLE 5 · THE FIRST MOVE

There are 30 sticks. How many do you take first?

$30 : 4 = 7$ remainder 2. Take 2, then 28 are left – a multiple of 4.

2 sticks

EXAMPLE 6 · MAKING IT UP

There are 16 sticks, and your opponent takes 3. How many do you take?

$3 + 1 = 4$, so 12 are left.

1 stick

EXERCISES

How many sticks do you take first with a) 15   b) 22   c) 25 sticks?

a) 3 (12 are left)   b) 2 (20 are left)   c) 1 (24 are left)

Play three times with 21 sticks in the interactive element. Note down how many sticks are left after each of your moves.

With the strategy: 20, 16, 12, 8, 4, 0 – you win.

There are 24 sticks and you are to start. What do you advise yourself?

24 is a multiple of 4. If your opponent plays perfectly, you lose – better to let the other person start. Otherwise take 1 and hope for a mistake.

New rule: you may take 1 to 4 sticks. There are 23. Find the winning strategy.

Now the multiples of 5 are losing positions. $23 : 5 = 4$ remainder 3: take 3, and 20 are left. Then always make it up to 5.

TEST YOURSELF!

30 sticks, take 1 to 3: how many do you take first?

$30 = 7 \cdot 4 + 2$

Your opponent takes 3. How many do you take to make it up to 4?

$4 - 3 = 1$

Rule take 1 to 4, 23 sticks: first move?

$23 = 4 \cdot 5 + 3$

UNIT 43 LESSONS

4Dice games and a game of your own

In the dice race the 7 wins most often, while the 2 and the 12 hardly move. Why? With two dice there are 36 equally likely outcomes: 6 possibilities for the first dice times 6 for the second.

The total 7 can be made in 6 ways: 1 + 6, 2 + 5, 3 + 4, 4 + 3, 5 + 2, 6 + 1. The total 2 in only one: 1 + 1. That is why the 7 comes up six times as often as the 2 – in the long run.

A game is fair if everyone has the same chance. If you invent a game of your own, you count the possibilities first.

KEY POINT · TWO DICE

36 outcomes, all equally likely · total scores 2 to 12

Number of possibilities: 2 and 12: 1 each · 7: 6 · chance of a 7: $\tfrac{6}{36} = \tfrac{1}{6}$

A game is fair if all the players have the same chance.

Red and blue: if you roll a red and a blue dice, you can see that 3 + 4 and 4 + 3 are two different outcomes.

A game of your own: write down the rules, play test rounds, count the chances, make it fair, present it to the class.

INTERACTIVE · TOTAL SCORES

Roll 100 times and compare the bars with the dashed lines. Tap a total: the matching cells light up.

EXAMPLE 7 · COUNTING

In how many ways can the total 9 be made? How big is the chance?

3 + 6, 4 + 5, 5 + 4, 6 + 3: 4 ways. Chance $\tfrac{4}{36} = \tfrac{1}{9}$.

4 out of 36, so $\tfrac{1}{9}$

EXAMPLE 8 · FAIR OR NOT?

Anna wins with a total of 2, 3, 4, 10, 11 or 12. Ben wins with 7. With all the other totals, you roll again. Who has the better chance?

Anna: $1 + 2 + 3 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 12$ cells. Ben: 6 cells.

Anna twice as good – the game is not fair.

EXERCISES

Write down all the possibilities for the total a) 4   b) 6   c) 11.

a) 1 + 3, 2 + 2, 3 + 1 (3 ways)   b) 1 + 5, 2 + 4, 3 + 3, 4 + 2, 5 + 1 (5 ways)   c) 5 + 6, 6 + 5 (2 ways)

Roll 100 times in the interactive element. Which total came up most often? Does that fit the cells in the grid?

Mostly the 7 or a neighbouring number (6, 8). The more rolls, the closer the bars come to the dashed lines.

Even or odd total: who has the better chance? Count in the grid.

Even: 18 cells, odd: 18 cells. The same chance – the game is fair.

Make the game from example 8 fair. Does it work if Anna keeps her totals and Ben wins with only one more total besides 7? Find a fair rule.

If Anna keeps her totals, it does not work with one total: Ben needs 6 more cells, and apart from 7 no total has 6 cells. A fair rule is, for example: Ben wins with 7 and 8 ($6 + 5 = 11$ cells), Anna with 2, 3, 4, 10 and 11 ($1 + 2 + 3 + 3 + 2 = 11$ cells), and with all the other totals you roll again.

TEST YOURSELF!

How many outcomes are there when rolling two dice?

$6 \cdot 6 = 36$

In how many ways can the total 9 be made?

3 + 6, 4 + 5, 5 + 4, 6 + 3

The chance of the total 7 as a fraction?

$\tfrac{6}{36} = \tfrac{1}{6}$

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

A tangram has a side length of 10 cm. How big is the small square in it? About how long is its side?

$\tfrac{1}{8}$ of 100 cm² = 12.5 cm². The side is about 3.5 cm, because $3.5 \cdot 3.5 = 12.25$.

For the Tower of Hanoi there is a mental shortcut: how many moves do you need with 7 discs? Calculate with the doubling rule and check with $2^7 - 1$.

63 → 127. $2^7 = 128$, $128 - 1 = 127$ ✓

Invent a dice game for two people with two dice that is fair. Write down the rules and justify them with the grid of 36 cells.

For example: A wins with an even total, B with an odd one – 18 cells each. Or: A wins if the red dice shows more, B if the blue dice shows more, and with a draw you roll again – 15 cells each.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

The Fifteen fever of 1880

Around 1874, Noyes Chapman, a postmaster from Canastota in the state of New York, showed his friends a little wooden box with 15 numbered tiles and a gap. By around 1880 the “Fifteen puzzle” was all the rage in America and Europe: people played it at home, in offices and in pubs.

One task was especially popular: everything is in place, only 14 and 15 are swapped. Countless people tried for hours. In vain: the mathematicians William Woolsey Johnson and William Edward Story proved in 1879 that exactly half of all arrangements can never be put in order – including this one.

Later the puzzle-maker Sam Loyd claimed that he had invented the game. That is not true – Jerry Slocum and Dic Sonneveld traced the story precisely in 2006.

Sources: W. W. Johnson, W. E. Story, “Notes on the ‘15’ Puzzle” I and II, American Journal of Mathematics 2 (1879); J. Slocum, D. Sonneveld, “The 15 Puzzle”, 2006.
